Title: How to Validate an Idea Before Writing Code
Desc: Learn practical ways to validate a startup, SaaS, app, or side-project idea before spending weeks or months building something nobody wants.
Author: Core Lord
Data:
One of the most expensive mistakes developers make is building first and validating later.

The pattern usually looks like this:

```text
Great Idea
↓
Weeks of Coding
↓
Launch
↓
No Users

The problem is rarely bad code.

The problem is often that nobody actually needed the solution.

Validating an idea before writing code can save:

Time

Money

Energy

Motivation


The goal is simple:

> Prove people want the solution before investing heavily in building it.




---

What Does Validation Mean?

Validation means collecting evidence that real people have a real problem and are interested in your solution.

Validation is not:

Asking friends if the idea is good

Getting likes on social media

Receiving compliments


Validation is discovering whether people are willing to:

Use it

Sign up for it

Test it

Recommend it

Pay for it


Those signals matter far more.


---

Start With the Problem

Many developers focus on ideas.

Successful founders focus on problems.

Instead of asking:

Is this app a good idea?

Ask:

Is this problem painful enough to solve?

The stronger the problem, the easier the product becomes to sell.


---



Identify Your Target Audience

Not everyone is your customer.

Define:

Who experiences the problem?

How often?

How severe is it?

What solutions do they currently use?


Examples:

Bad:

Everyone with a computer

Good:

Freelance web developers managing multiple clients

Specific audiences are easier to validate.


---

Talk to Potential Users

The fastest validation tool is conversation.

Ask potential users:

What frustrates you?

How do you solve this today?

What do you dislike about current solutions?

How much time does this problem cost?


Avoid asking:

Would you use my app?

People often say yes to be polite.

Focus on their current behavior instead.


---

Look for Existing Solutions

Competition is usually a good sign.

Many developers fear competition.

In reality, competition often means:

People Already Pay
↓
Market Exists

Research:

Existing products

Pricing models

Reviews

Complaints


Complaints often reveal opportunities.


---

Search Communities

Places to explore include:

Reddit

GitHub discussions

Developer forums

Discord communities

Facebook groups

Product communities


Look for repeated complaints.

When dozens of people complain about the same thing, validation may already exist.


---



Build a Landing Page First

Instead of building software, build a simple landing page.

Include:

Problem statement

Proposed solution

Benefits

Call to action


Example:

Join the Waitlist

or

Get Early Access

This measures actual interest.


---

Track Sign-Ups

A landing page becomes useful when you collect data.

Metrics include:

Visitors

Sign-ups

Conversion rate

Feedback


Example:

500 Visitors
↓
75 Sign-Ups

This provides stronger validation than opinions.


---

Create a Clickable Mockup

Many ideas can be tested without writing production code.

Tools allow you to create:

Wireframes

Mockups

Interactive prototypes


Users can react to the experience before development begins.

Benefits:

Faster feedback

Lower cost

Easier iteration



---

Pre-Sell the Idea

One of the strongest validation signals is payment.

If people are willing to pay before the product exists, that's powerful evidence.

Examples:

Pre-orders

Founding memberships

Early access plans


Revenue validates interest more effectively than compliments.


---



Build the Smallest Possible Version

Avoid building every feature.

Instead:

Idea
↓
MVP
↓
Feedback

MVP stands for Minimum Viable Product.

The goal is learning, not perfection.


---

Measure Real Behavior

Pay attention to actions rather than opinions.

Strong signals:

Sign-ups

Purchases

Referrals

Repeat usage

Engagement


Weak signals:

Likes

Compliments

"Sounds cool"


Actions matter more than words.


---

Watch for Problem Intensity

Not all problems are worth solving.

Ask:

Is this problem frequent?

Is it expensive?

Is it frustrating?

Do people actively seek solutions?


The more painful the problem, the easier validation becomes.


---

Common Validation Mistakes

Building Too Much

Many developers spend months building features nobody requested.

Validate first.


---

Asking Leading Questions

Example:

Wouldn't this app be useful?

This encourages biased responses.


---

Only Talking to Friends

Friends often provide supportive rather than honest feedback.

Seek real users.


---

Ignoring Competition

Competition provides valuable market information.


---

Chasing Vanity Metrics

Traffic without engagement rarely proves demand.

Focus on meaningful actions.


---



A Simple Validation Framework

Use this process:

Identify Problem
↓
Find Audience
↓
Talk to Users
↓
Research Competition
↓
Create Landing Page
↓
Collect Sign-Ups
↓
Build MVP
↓
Measure Usage

Each step reduces risk.


---

Signs Your Idea Is Validated

Positive indicators include:

Users actively discuss the problem

Existing solutions have paying customers

People join your waitlist

Users request updates

Customers are willing to pay


These signals are far more valuable than enthusiasm alone.


---

When to Start Coding

Start building when you have evidence.

Examples:

Multiple user interviews

Consistent feedback patterns

Waitlist growth

Pre-orders

Early commitments


Evidence reduces guesswork.


---

FAQ

How much validation is enough?

There is no perfect number, but multiple independent signals are better than relying on a single source.

Should I build an MVP immediately?

Usually after validating the problem and audience first.

Is competition a bad sign?

No. Competition often indicates an existing market.

What is the strongest validation signal?

People spending money or making commitments.

Can I validate without coding?

Absolutely. Landing pages, interviews, prototypes, and pre-sales are common validation methods.


---

Final Thoughts

The best way to avoid building something nobody wants is to validate before you code.

Talk to users, research existing solutions, create simple prototypes, test demand, and gather evidence. The goal is not proving your idea is perfect—it's proving that a real problem exists and that people care enough to solve it.

Code is expensive. Learning is cheaper.

The most successful products are often built by teams that spend as much time validating as they do developing.
